title: Reality and Consciousness
content_html:
Reality and Consciousness

What we call “reality” is always given through conscious experience. There is no access to a “pure” external reality independent of consciousness. But perception is not passive; the brain constructs sensory experience based on prior models, expectations, and memory. Consciousness is the brain’s generative model; what we perceive is largely top-down inference constrained by sensory data. In these accounts: reality-for-us is literally created by consciousness. “to be is to be perceived” (esse est percipi) - reality is sustained by being in consciousness, and the structure of the world is shaped by the structure of mind. Consciousness is the primary ontological reality; the material world is derivative, reality itself is consciousness.

Observers “bring reality into being” by collapsing quantum possibilities, quantum states are not external but represent the agent’s expectations; reality emerges from interaction and subjective updating. This does not prove consciousness creates reality, but they blur the line between observation and being. Here, measurement/experience co-defines reality at the fundamental level; reality is incomplete without observers.

Buddhist traditions argue that what we call “reality” is inseparable from, or even generated by, consciousness.

Madhyamaka (Nāgārjuna): phenomena are empty of inherent existence, they arise only in dependence (mind–world co-arising).
Yogācāra (mind-only school): what we take as external reality is projection of consciousness streams.
